title: ng nk th sh ch
overview:
New sounds: ng, nk, th, sh, ch.
Five pairs. Each one is a sound you have not read before.
Two letters. One sound.
Do not sound them out one by one.
functions: Say the sound for each new spelling
Read a word that has one in it
Write a word that has one in it
Know where in a word each one goes
Read the new words out loud
Choose between two spellings of one sound
learningPath: Words: the new sounds and the new words.
Write the words from their sounds.
Practice and quiz. Check your answers.
lectureScript:
This is Unit 12. Five new sounds.
Each one is written with two letters.
Two letters. One sound. Like ck in Unit 8.
But these five are sounds that are new.
The first is ng. Listen. ng.
It comes at the END of a word.
Sing. s. i. ng. Three sounds.
Not s, i, n, g. Three, not four.
Next is nk. Listen. nk.
Also at the end. Bank. b. a. nk.
Sing and sink. Listen again. Sing. Sink.
Now th. Listen. th.
This one is special. It says two sounds.
Listen. Thin. Now listen. This.
Thin and this. Not the same.
Put your hand on your throat.
Say thin. Nothing moves.
Say this. It buzzes under your hand.
Same two letters. Two sounds.
Do not stop to pick one.
Say the word. Your mouth will find it.
Next is sh. Listen. sh.
Shop. sh. o. p. Three sounds.
It can go at the end too. Cash.
Last is ch. Listen. ch.
Chin. ch. i. n. Three sounds.
And at the end. Much. m. u. ch.
Now three very common words.
That. Them. With.
All three have th in them.
And all three follow the sounds.
That is th, a, t. Them is th, e, m.
With is w, i, th.
They are not tricky. You can read them.
Those are three of the commonest words there are.
That is Unit 12. Two letters. One sound.

grammar.title: The new sounds: ng, nk, th, sh, ch
grammar.explanation:
Each pair is ONE sound.
The sound is new. You have not read it before.
Say one sound, never two.
grammar.rule:
ng   as in sing     end only
nk   as in bank     end only
th   as in thin     anywhere
sh   as in shop     start or end
ch   as in chin     start or end
grammar.workedExample:
You see ng in a word.
1. Do not read two letters.
2. Read one sound.
3. Say that sound out loud.
4. Now find it in sing.
5. Say the sound again there.
grammar.mistake:
Sounding out both letters gives no word at all.
sing is not s - i - n - g.
It is s - i - ng.
grammar.tip: Two letters. Look once. Say once.
grammar.practice:
Say the sound for each one.
1. ng
2. nk
3. th
4. sh
5. ch
grammar.answers:
Check yourself out loud.
Did you say ONE sound each time?
Two sounds means you read the letters, not the spelling.

grammar.title: Reading a word that has ng, nk, th, sh, ch in it
grammar.explanation:
Find the two letters first.
Read them as one sound.
Then read the rest of the word.
grammar.rule:
sing     s - i - ng
bank     b - a - nk
thin     th - i - n
this     th - i - s
shop     sh - o - p
chin     ch - i - n
grammar.workedExample:
You see the word bank.
1. Look for the two letters.
2. Cover them with your finger.
3. Read what is left.
4. Now put the one sound back in.
5. Join it all. bank.
grammar.mistake:
Reading left to right, letter by letter, breaks here.
Look for the pair BEFORE you start.
grammar.practice:
Join the sounds and write the word.
1. s - i - ng
2. b - a - nk
3. th - i - n
4. th - i - s
5. sh - o - p
6. ch - i - n
grammar.answers:
1. sing
2. bank
3. thin
4. this
5. shop
6. chin
Five or six right? You can read these.

grammar.title: Writing a word that has ng, nk, th, sh, ch in it
grammar.explanation:
Say the word. Break it into sounds.
One of those sounds needs TWO letters.
Count sounds, then write.
grammar.rule:
sing     s - i - ng         3 sounds, 4 letters
bank     b - a - nk         3 sounds, 4 letters
grammar.workedExample:
You want to write thin.
1. Say it out loud.
2. Break it: th - i - n.
3. Which sound needs two letters?
4. Write that pair together.
5. Read it back to check.
grammar.mistake:
One letter for each sound is wrong now.
The new sound takes two letters.
grammar.tip: Count sounds. Some need two letters.
grammar.practice:
Write the word you hear.
1. thin
2. this
3. shop
4. chin
5. cash
6. much
grammar.answers:
1. thin
2. this
3. shop
4. chin
5. cash
6. much
Five or six right? Good.

grammar.title: Where each spelling goes
grammar.explanation:
Two of them only ever come at the end.
The other three can move.
Knowing this saves you looking.
grammar.rule:
ng   end only        sing, long
nk   end only        bank, think
sh   start or end    shop, cash
ch   start or end    chin, much
th   anywhere        thin, with
grammar.workedExample:
You think a word starts with ng.
1. Stop. That does not happen.
2. No English word starts with ng.
3. Look again at the letters.
4. It is n and g in two parts.
5. Or it is not ng at all.
grammar.mistake:
Hunting for ng at the start wastes time.
It is never there. Look at the end.
grammar.tip: ng and nk live at the end.
grammar.practice:
Where is the new spelling? Start or end?
1. sing
2. shop
3. bank
4. cash
5. chin
6. much
grammar.answers:
1. end
2. start
3. end
4. end
5. start
6. end
Five or six right? You know where to look.

grammar.title: Quiet th and buzzing th, and the words that use them
grammar.explanation:
th is one spelling and two sounds.
Your mouth already makes both.
You do not choose. The word chooses.
grammar.rule:
Quiet th     thin, three, with
Buzzing th   this, that, them

that, them, with, this
Four of the commonest words in English.
grammar.workedExample:
Put a hand on your throat.
1. Say thin. Feel nothing.
2. Say this. Feel a buzz.
3. Same letters. Different sound.
4. Do not stop to decide.
5. Say the word and it comes out right.
grammar.mistake:
Treating that, them and with as tricky words is wrong.
They follow the sounds. Read them.
grammar.tip: Same spelling. Two sounds. Say the word.
grammar.practice:
Quiet or buzzing? Hand on your throat.
1. thin
2. this
3. that
4. with
5. them
6. three
grammar.answers:
1. quiet
2. buzzing
3. buzzing
4. quiet
5. buzzing
6. quiet
Five or six right? Good ears.

readings.title: The Shop by the Bank
readings.genre: A short text using known sounds
readings.setting: A row of shops, on a wet afternoon
readings.passage:
I went to the shop.
The shop is next to the bank.
I had a bit of cash with me.
A man in the shop did sing.
It was a long, thin song.
I got a big fish and went back.
I think that shop is the best.

speaking.title: Speaking 1 — The new sounds
speaking.instructions:
Listen and repeat each sound.
ng
nk
th
sh
ch
ONE sound each. Not two.
Now say each one three times.
Tap the mic. Say them all.
Check: one sound, or did two slip out?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say one of the new sounds. Say it back.

speaking.title: Speaking 2 — Read the words
speaking.instructions:
Say each word two ways. Slow, then fast.
1. s - i - ng ... sing
2. b - a - nk ... bank
3. th - i - n ... thin
4. th - i - s ... this
5. sh - o - p ... shop
6. ch - i - n ... chin
Tap the mic. Say all six both ways.
Check: was the new spelling one sound?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say three sounds. Join them and say the word.

speaking.title: Speaking 3 — Say it, then write it
speaking.instructions:
For each word: say it, break it, write it.
1. thin
2. this
3. shop
4. chin
5. cash
6. much
Tap the mic. Say each word and its sounds.
Check: did you say the sounds before you wrote?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word with the new spelling. Break it out loud.

speaking.title: Speaking 4 — Read the list
speaking.instructions:
Read these out loud, straight down the list.
sing
bank
thin
this
shop
chin
cash
much
Do it twice. The second time, try not to stop.
Tap the mic. Read the list twice.
Check: was the second time easier?
speaking.tutor: Read the list to the tutor. Ask which words were not clear.

speaking.title: Speaking 5 — Start or end?
speaking.instructions:
Say each word. Then say where the spelling is.
sing. shop. bank. cash. chin. much.
Say the word, then say start or end.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: were ng and nk both at the end?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor for a word that ends in ng.

speaking.title: Speaking 6 — Quiet th and buzzing th
speaking.instructions:
Put a hand on your throat. Say each word.
thin. this. that. with. them. three.
Say quiet or buzzing after each one.
Tap the mic. Do all six.
Check: did you feel the difference?
speaking.tutor: Ask the tutor to say this and thin. Listen for the buzz.

quizzes.why: Read the pair as one, not as two letters.

quizzes.why: The sounds in order make the word.

quizzes.q: Join the sounds: b - a - nk. The word is ___.
quizzes.why: Find the pair first, then read the rest.

quizzes.q: To write a word with the new spelling you ___.
options: write two letters for that sound
write one letter for each sound
quizzes.a: write two letters for that sound
quizzes.why: The new sound is one sound and two letters.

quizzes.q: How many sounds are in sing?
quizzes.why: Count what you HEAR. There are more letters than sounds.

options: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.a: read the pair as one sound
quizzes.why: Letter by letter is the slow way here.

quizzes.q: You cannot read a word. What do you do first?
quizzes.why: Find the pair, then read around it.

quizzes.why: sh is first. The other three have theirs at the end.

teacherNotes.note: Every pattern card has a worked example, every practice has a key, and every speaking task ends with record, listen back, check.

This is the whole unit, and it goes against everything Units 2 to 7 taught. Expect a learner to read the letters separately for a while. Do not explain it again; point at the pair and say the one sound, and have them say it back. It is a habit, and habits are built by repetition, not by argument.

teacherNotes.type: Find the pair before reading, not during
teacherNotes.note: Left-to-right letter-by-letter reading breaks on these words, because the learner commits to the first letter's sound before they have seen the second. The move is to scan the word for the pair first. A finger under the pair is enough. It looks like a crutch and it is the skill.

From here to the end of the level there are always more letters than sounds. A learner who counts letters will write a spare letter into every word. Have them say the word and count on their fingers before they write.

teacherNotes.type: ng and nk are the pair learners confuse
teacherNotes.note: They differ by one small sound at the end, and a learner whose first language does not use both will hear them as the same. Say sing and sink slowly, side by side, and have them listen for the k rather than for the whole word. Do not drill it to perfection: reading them correctly in context comes first.

teacherNotes.type: that, them and with are NOT tricky words
teacherNotes.note: The plan called them tricky; they are not, and the unit says so. All three follow the sounds once th is known, and proving that is worth more than the three words themselves. If a learner tries to memorise them by shape, stop and sound them out together.

teacherNotes.type: Do not teach which th is which
teacherNotes.note: The quiet and buzzing th are allophones of a spelling, not a choice the reader makes. Adults who are told to pick one hesitate before every th word. The card exists so they know the two sounds are normal, not so they can predict them.

assignment.title: Read and write the new words
assignment.instructions:
Two parts.
1. Record yourself. Say the sound for each new spelling.
Then read these words, slowly and then faster:
sing, bank, thin, this, shop, chin
2. Write six of the words from their sounds.
Beside each one, write how many sounds it has.
Listen back before you finish.
